subject: maths
title: Chapter 11 · Test 4
summary: Chapter 11 test 4: searching and sorting algorithms, recurrence rules, iteration and approximation — 15 questions.
body: This test covers Chapter 11 · Algorithmic thinking: linear and binary search, bubble sort and selection sort, counting comparisons, recurrence rules, the Babylonian method for square roots, fixed-point iteration, the halving method and stopping rules. Allow about 25 minutes, no notes, no calculator unless the question says. Some questions show the list or graph in a diagram — read it carefully. Work each question out on paper before you look at the options, and write your steps so you can find where you went wrong.

questions.prompt: Linear search is used to find 10 in the list shown in the diagram. How many comparisons are made, including the one that finds 10?
questions.explanation: Linear search checks from the left: 21, 13, 44, 6, 35, 29, 10 — 10 is found on comparison 7. 6 forgets to count the comparison that finds it.
steps: Linear search starts with the first item and checks each item in turn.
The items checked are 21, 13, 44, 6, 35, 29, 10, so 10 is found on comparison 7.

mistakes.A: Step 2: count the comparison with 10 itself as well — that is the one that finds it.
mistakes.C: Step 2: linear search stops as soon as it finds 10; it does not check the rest of the list.
mistakes.D: Step 1: linear search starts at the first item on the left, not at the end of the list.

questions.diagram_alt: A list of 9 boxes holding 21, 13, 44, 6, 35, 29, 10, 52, 3, with positions 1 to 9 underneath.

questions.prompt: Before binary search can be used on a list, what must be true about the list?

options.A: It must have an odd number of items
options.B: The target must be in the middle
options.C: It must have fewer than 100 items
options.D: It must be sorted into order

questions.explanation: Binary search throws away half the list after each look, which is only safe if the list is in order. The number of items does not matter.
steps: After each look, binary search keeps only the half that could hold the target.
That only works if everything on one side is smaller and everything on the other side is bigger — the list must be sorted.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the middle is found by rounding (low + high) ÷ 2, so any number of items works.
mistakes.B: Step 1: the middle is only where binary search starts looking; the target can be anywhere.
mistakes.C: Step 2: binary search works on lists of any size — it is most useful on very long lists.

questions.prompt: A sequence follows the rule uₙ₊₁ = 3uₙ + 5 with u₀ = 1. Find u₂.
questions.explanation: u₁ = 3 × 1 + 5 = 8 and u₂ = 3 × 8 + 5 = 29. 8 stops after one step.
steps: u₁ = 3 × 1 + 5 = 8 — substitute u₀ into the rule.
u₂ = 3 × 8 + 5 = 29 — feed u₁ back into the rule.

mistakes.B: Step 1: 8 is only u₁. Use the rule a second time to get u₂.
mistakes.C: Step 1: multiply by 3 first, then add 5 — you did them in the wrong order.
mistakes.D: Step 2: that is u₃ — you used the rule one time too many.

questions.prompt: The halving method is used on f(x) = x³ − 50. The diagram shows f(3), f(3.5) and f(4). After this halving, which interval contains the solution?
questions.explanation: The sign changes in the interval 3.5 to 4, so the graph crosses zero there. 3 to 3.5 has no sign change.
steps: Look at the signs: f(3) = −23 is negative, f(4) = 14 is positive and f(3.5) = −7.125 is negative.
The sign changes between 3.5 and 4, so the solution is in the interval 3.5 to 4.

mistakes.A: Step 2: keep the half where the signs are DIFFERENT. f(3) and f(3.5) have the same sign.
mistakes.B: Step 2: after finding f(3.5), update the interval to half its width.
mistakes.D: Step 2: only one halving is asked for — you cannot narrow it further without another function value.

questions.diagram_alt: A number line from 3 to 4 with f(3) = −23, f(3.5) = −7.125 and f(4) = 14 marked.

questions.prompt: Binary search is used to find 20 in the sorted list shown. The middle position is (low + high) ÷ 2, rounded down. Which numbers are compared with 20, in order?
questions.explanation: Halving from the middle each time compares 26, 12, 17, 20. Rounding the middle up instead gives 28, 17, 26, 20.
steps: Middle of 1 to 10 is position 5, which holds 26. 20 is smaller, so keep positions 1 to 4.
Middle of 1 to 4 is position 2, which holds 12. 20 is bigger, so keep positions 3 to 4.
Middle of 3 to 4 is position 3, which holds 17. 20 is bigger, so keep position 4.
Position 4 is all that is left; it holds 20 — found. So the order is 26, 12, 17, 20.

mistakes.A: Step 2: when (low + high) ÷ 2 is not a whole number, round it DOWN, not up.
mistakes.B: Step 2: after the first look, find the middle of the part that is left — do not step along one item at a time.
mistakes.C: Step 1: that is linear search. Binary search starts by looking at the middle position.

questions.diagram_alt: A sorted list of 10 boxes: 7, 12, 17, 20, 26, 28, 35, 39, 44, 51, with positions 1 to 10 underneath.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows the list 9, 2, 7, 4, 6, 1 before bubble sort starts (sorting into increasing order). What is the list after the first pass?
questions.explanation: Walking along and swapping each out-of-order pair gives 2, 7, 4, 6, 1, 9 — the largest value, 9, ends at the back. 2, 4, 6, 1, 7, 9 is after two passes.
steps: Compare 9 and 2: swap → 2, 9, 7, 4, 6, 1. Compare 9 and 7: swap → 2, 7, 9, 4, 6, 1. Compare 9 and 4: swap → 2, 7, 4, 9, 6, 1.
Compare 9 and 6: swap → 2, 7, 4, 6, 9, 1. Compare 9 and 1: swap → 2, 7, 4, 6, 1, 9.

mistakes.A: Step 2: one pass does not sort the whole list — it only makes sure the largest value reaches the end.
mistakes.B: Step 2: that is after the SECOND pass. Stop after one walk along the list.
mistakes.D: Step 1: keep going after the first swap — compare every neighbouring pair along the list.

questions.prompt: A sorted list has 40 items. What is the greatest number of comparisons binary search could need?
questions.explanation: Find the smallest k with 2ᵏ ≥ 41: 2⁵ = 32 is too small and 2⁶ = 64 is enough, so 6.
steps: Binary search worst case: the smallest whole number k with 2ᵏ ≥ n + 1 = 41.
2⁵ = 32 is too small, but 2⁶ = 64 ≥ 41, so the answer is 6.

mistakes.A: Step 1: binary search halves the list every look — 20 is just half the list after one look.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 40 is the worst case for linear search, not binary search.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 2⁵ = 32 is less than 41, so 5 looks are not enough. Round up, not down.

questions.prompt: A bank account follows Bₙ₊₁ = 1.01Bₙ + 250 each month (250 dollars deposited each month), where B₀ = $3000. Find B₂, the balance after 2 months.
questions.explanation: B₁ = 1.01 × 3000 + 250 = 3280.00 and B₂ = 1.01 × 3280.00 + 250 = 3562.80. $3560.00 wrongly earns interest on the original balance both months.

mistakes.B: Step 1: the rule multiplies by 1.01 each month — you left out the interest.
mistakes.C: Step 2: the interest in month 2 is on $3280.00, not on the original $3000.
mistakes.D: Step 1: $3280.00 is only after one month. Use the rule again for B₂.

questions.prompt: The iteration xₙ₊₁ = 4 + 12 ÷ xₙ settles at a value of x. Which equation does that value solve?
questions.explanation: At the fixed point the new and old values are equal, which leads to x² − 4x − 12 = 0 (its positive solution is 6).
steps: When the iterates settle at x, the rule says x = 4 + 12 ÷ x.
Multiply every term by x: x² = 4x + 12.
Move everything to one side: x² − 4x − 12 = 0.

mistakes.B: Step 2: multiply EVERY term by x: 4 × x = 4x, and (12 ÷ x) × x = 12.
mistakes.C: Step 3: subtract 12 from both sides, so the constant becomes −12.
mistakes.D: Step 2: the left side, x, must be multiplied by x too, giving x².

questions.prompt: Selection sort is used on the list 6, 9, 3, 7, 2, 5, shown in the diagram (sorting into increasing order). What is the list after the second pass?
questions.explanation: Two passes place 2 and then 3 at the front: 2, 3, 9, 7, 6, 5. 3, 6, 2, 5, 7, 9 is what bubble sort gives after two passes.
steps: Pass 1: the smallest of all is 2 — swap it with the first item, 6: 2, 9, 3, 7, 6, 5.
Pass 2: the smallest of 9, 3, 7, 6, 5 is 3 — swap it with 9: 2, 3, 9, 7, 6, 5.

mistakes.A: Step 2: two passes only fix the first two positions — the rest is not sorted yet.
mistakes.B: Step 1: that is after one pass. Do a second pass on the items after the first.
mistakes.C: Step 1: that is bubble sort after two passes. Selection sort moves the smallest remaining item to the front.

questions.prompt: A sorted list holds 3000 names, and a name that is NOT in the list is searched for. How many more comparisons does linear search need than binary search, in the worst case?
questions.explanation: Linear search checks all 3000. Binary search needs the smallest k with 2ᵏ ≥ 3001, which is 12 (2¹² = 4096). 3000 − 12 = 2988.
steps: Linear search: a missing name means all 3000 names are checked.
Binary search: 2¹¹ = 2048 is too small, 2¹² = 4096 ≥ 3001, so 12 comparisons.
Difference: 3000 − 12 = 2988.

mistakes.A: Step 1: the worst case for linear search is all 3000 items, not half of them.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 2¹¹ = 2048 is less than 3001, so binary search needs 12 looks, not 11.
mistakes.D: Step 2: binary search halves the list on every look — it needs far fewer than half the items.

questions.prompt: The halving method starts with the interval 1 to 3. How many halvings are needed to make the interval narrower than 0.01?
questions.explanation: After n halvings the width is 2 ÷ 2ⁿ, so we need 2ⁿ greater than 200: 2⁷ = 128 is too small and 2⁸ = 256 works, so 8.
steps: After n halvings the width is 2 ÷ 2ⁿ, so 2ⁿ must be greater than 2 ÷ 0.01 = 200.
2⁷ = 128 is too small; 2⁸ = 256 is big enough, so 8 halvings.

mistakes.A: Step 1: halving does not add one decimal place each time — each step only halves the width.
mistakes.B: Step 1: the interval from 1 to 3 has width 2, not 1.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 200 is how many pieces of width 0.01 fit in the interval. Each halving doubles the pieces, so far fewer steps are needed.

questions.prompt: A loan of $12 000 follows Lₙ₊₁ = 1.005Lₙ − 600, where n is the number of months (0.5% interest per month and a $600 repayment). After how many months is the balance first below $9200?
questions.explanation: Working month by month, L₅ ≈ $9272.86 is still above $9200 but L₆ ≈ $8719.23 is below, so 6 months. Ignoring the interest gives 5.

mistakes.B: Step 1: the rule multiplies by the interest factor before taking off the repayment — without interest the balance falls too quickly.
mistakes.C: Step 2: L₀ is the starting balance, not month 1. Count from L₁.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 0.5% per month is ×1.005, not ×1.05. With ×1.05 the interest would cancel the repayment every month.

questions.prompt: Binary search must always find a target, or show it is missing, in at most 5 comparisons. What is the largest sorted list it can be used on?
questions.explanation: With k looks binary search handles up to 2ᵏ − 1 items: 2⁵ − 1 = 31. With 32 items, 2⁵ = 32 is less than 33, so 6 looks could be needed.
steps: The worst case for n items is the smallest k with 2ᵏ ≥ n + 1, so we need n + 1 ≤ 2⁵ = 32.

mistakes.A: Step 2: binary search needs 2ᵏ ≥ n + 1, not 2ᵏ ≥ n. With 32 items it could need 6 looks.
mistakes.C: Step 1: each look halves the list — the size grows like a power of 2, not like 5².
mistakes.D: Step 1: each extra look DOUBLES the list size it can handle, it does not add 2.

questions.prompt: A population follows Pₙ₊₁ = 0.75Pₙ + 120 (each year 25% leave and 120 arrive). What steady-state value does the population settle at?
questions.explanation: At the steady state L = 0.75L + 120, so 0.25L = 120 and L = 480. 160 divides by 0.75 instead of 0.25.
steps: At the steady state the population does not change, so L = 0.75L + 120.

mistakes.A: Step 2: from L = 0.75L + 120, subtract 0.75L to get 0.25L = 120 — divide by 0.25, not by 0.75.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 0.75L must be SUBTRACTED from both sides, not added.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 0.75 × 120 is just part of the rule. Set Pₙ₊₁ and Pₙ both equal to L and solve.
